narrative:
The law school admission decision was based on a prediction that you have a 66.8 percent chance of failing the bar exam on the first attempt. In other words, based on how past students with similar records performed, the model saw a clear majority chance you would not pass, and that risk drove the rejection.

The most decisive factor was your class standing in the third year. You ranked in the lowest decile of your school in Year 3, while admitted students typically land near the middle of the distribution, around the sixth decile. That steep gap was the single strongest signal pushing toward bar exam failure, because third-year performance is the most reliable mirror of how well you absorb and retain legal material.

Your first-year class standing also pushed toward failure, but with less impact. You were in the fourth decile versus an average of the sixth decile among accepted applicants. That is below the admitted cohort, but not as extreme as your third-year position.

Interestingly, your LSAT score of 36, slightly below the average of 37.18, actually nudged the prediction toward passing. This suggests raw aptitude was not the problem; the concern is sustained performance during your legal studies.

If you reapply, show the committee that your recent record has changed direction. Consider retaking courses, obtaining strong recommendations from third-year professors, and raising your LSAT to strengthen that already positive signal. Above all, address the academic decline that the model flagged.
